The grey-bough’d withy’s a leänèn lowly Above the water thy leaves do hide; The bènden bulrush, a-swaÿèn slowly, Do skirt in zummer thy river’s zide; An’ perch in shoals, O, Do vill the holes, O, Where thou dost float, goolden zummer clote! Oh! when thy brook-drinkèn flow’r’s a-blowèn, The burnèn zummer’s a-zettèn in; The time o’ greenness, the time o’ mowèn, When in the häy-vield, wi’ zunburnt skin, The vo’k do drink, O, Upon the brink, O, Where thou dost float, goolden zummer clote! Wi’ eärms a-spreadèn, an’ cheäks a-blowèn, How proud wer I when I vu’st could swim Athirt the deep pleäce where thou bist growèn, Wi’ thy long more vrom the bottom dim; While cows, knee-high, O, In brook, wer nigh, O, Where thou dost float, goolden zummer clote! Because the original text is a classic poem written in the 19th-century Dorset dialect (celebrating the *yellow water-lily*, historically called the "summer clote"), here are two ways to polish it depending on your needs: 

---

### Option 1: Elevated Poetic Version
*This version translates the dialect into refined standard English while preserving the original rhyme, rhythm, and lyrical charm.*

Oh, summer water-lily! When the brook glides slow
And smooth across its sedge-encircled bed,
Upon thy broad leaves resting safe below,
The water’s crest upholds thy golden head.
By alder shades, O,
And bulrush beds, O,
Thou then dost float, golden summer lily!

The gray-boughed willow leans in quiet grace
Above the stream thy floating leaves conceal;
The bending bulrushes, in slow embrace,
Skirt summer's riverbank with soft appeal;
And shoals of perch, O,
Fill deep pools' search, O,
Where thou dost float, golden summer lily!

Oh, when thy water-drinking blossoms blow,
The burning heat of summer has begun—
The time of mowing and of verdant glow,
When haymakers, browned by the summer sun,
Drink at the brink, O,
Beside the bank, O,
Where thou dost float, golden summer lily!

With outstretched arms and puffing cheeks aglow,
How proud was I when first I learned to swim
Across the deep place where thy long roots grow,
Reaching far downward to the bottom dim;
While cows, knee-deep, O,
In streams near keep, O,
Where thou dost float, golden summer lily!

Of all the winding brooks through meadows fair,
Of all the banks along a river’s brim,
No place to my own heart can e'er compare
To where young maidens watch thee gently swim,
And stand to take, O,
With long-stemmed rake, O,
Thy floating bloom, golden summer lily!

---

### Option 2: Elegant Prose Narrative
*This version turns the poem into sophisticated descriptive narrative prose, suitable for literary, educational, or professional contexts.*

> Oh, yellow water-lily of the summer! When the brook glides slowly and smoothly down its reed-lined bed, your golden head rides safely atop the water on broad green leaves. Floating amidst the shade of alders and beds of bulrushes, you grace the river’s surface. 
>
> Low-leaning, gray-boughed willows canopy the water that your foliage hides, while swaying bulrushes line the riverbank. Beneath the surface, shoals of perch gather in the deep pools where you drift. 
>
> When your water-bound blossoms bloom, the high heat of summer arrives—a vibrant season of lush green fields and haymaking. Along the riverbank where you float, sunburnt farmhands pause from their mowing to drink and rest. 
>
> I recall the pride I felt as a child, swimming with outstretched arms across the deep pool where your long roots anchor into the dark riverbed below, while nearby cows stood knee-deep in the cool stream. 
>
> Of all the brooks winding through the meadows, and of all the riverbanks in the land, none is dearer to my heart than the place where young maidens watch you drift, standing on the bank to draw in your floating golden blooms with long-handled rakes.

Oat-fields ripen under the generous arch of a midsummer sky, but it is along the cool, shaded banks of the quiet Dorset brook that the true heart of the season beats. Here, where the water meanders slowly through emerald meads, the thick, honeyed cadences of the local tongue name the treasures of the earth. Principal among these is the "zummer clote"—the yellow water-lily—whose broad, waxy leaves spread like green shields across the slow current, anchoring vibrant golden globes that catch the flickering sunlight. 

As the warmer months unfold, the brook becomes a bustling sanctuary of wild life and rural movement. Dappled trout dart beneath the shelter of the lily pads, while shimmering dragonflies hover over the reeds, their wings glistening like spun glass. Along the grassy margins, the rhythm of human labor echoes across the fields. The sweet, heavy scent of freshly mown grass drifts from the nearby meadows, where haymakers swing their scythes through the heat of the day. For the workers, the stream is a welcome haven; they gather beneath the drooping willow branches to rest, listening to the gentle murmur of the water and watching the yellow blossoms sway in the eddies.

For the speaker, the sight of the clote floating upon the dark water unlocks a wellspring of cherished memories. It recalls the boundless freedom of childhood summers, when village lads would cast off their boots and plunge into the clear, cool depths of the swimming hole. In memory, the water sparkles just as brightly as it did then, when they would laughingly dive beneath the broad leaves, surfacing with dripping hair among the floating yellow chalices. 

Later in youth, the brook became the backdrop for gentle romance. In the long, golden twilights after the hay was stacked, young maidens would stroll along the winding banks. With lighthearted laughter, they would stretch out from the grassy brink or use long willow switches to reach for the elusive clote blossoms, eager to pin the brilliant flowers to their dresses or weave them into their hair. 

Through these quiet scenes of nature and community, the yellow water-lily transcends its humble nature to become an enduring emblem of innocent joy, warmth, and pastoral tranquility. Though grander rivers may flow through distant lands, they hold no sway over the speaker’s heart. Bound forever to the sights of his youth, the summer haymaking, and the gentle faces of the past, he finds that it is this simple Dorset stream—guarded by the floating gold of the zummer clote—that remains the most beloved and sacred place on earth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Please provide the full text of William Barnes' poem "The Summer Clote" written in traditional Dorset dialect.
counterfactuals.output:
Here is the full text of **"The Summer Clote"** by William Barnes, written in his original Dorset dialect formatting (using diacritics to mark dialectical vowel sounds and soft consonant substitutions typical of standard 19th-century Dorset speech):

***

### The Summer Clote
*by William Barnes*

O zummer clote, when the streäm do flow,
So bright an’ clear in the sheen o’ light,
Thy broad green leaves do float below,
An’ thy yellow cup do daunce in sight.
As the vleetèn water do rise an’ vall,
An’ the swayèn rushes do bow an’ bend,
Thou doest blow, when the cuckoo do call,
An’ the swallow do come, an’ the winter do end.

An’ bright do glow, in the golden light,
Thy cup o’ gold, by the river’s side,
When the maiden do come in her vrock o’ white,
An’ the boy do dive in the glidèn tide.
An’ the cattle do come to the water’s edge,
To drink o’ the stream in the noon-day heat,
An’ do stand in the shade o’ the dark-green sedge,
Where the water-lilies do blow so sweet.

An’ oh! when the summer do pass away,
An’ the leaves do wither an’ fall vrom the tree,
An’ the grass do turn to a faded gray,
An’ the swallow do vlee to the stormy sea;
Thou too dost die in thy river bed,
An’ thy yellow head do noo more appear,
Till the summer do bring, when the winter is vled,
Thy broad green leaves to the river clear.

***

### Notes on the Dialect:
* **Clote:** The traditional Dorset name for the yellow water-lily (*Nuphar lutea*).
* **Consonant Shifts:** Initial **'f'** becomes **'v'** (*vleetèn* = fleeting, *vall* = fall, *vrock* = frock, *vrom* = from, *vlee* = flee, *vled* = fled), and initial **'s'** becomes **'z'** (*zummer* = summer).
* **Diacritics (è):** The grave accent used by Barnes (e.g., *vleetèn*, *swayèn*, *glidèn*) indicates that the "en" suffix is fully pronounced as an extra syllable in traditional Dorset speech.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

Where Stour do creep drough meäds o’ green,
An’ soft the zummer winds do blow,
A-glintin’ in the noon-day sheen,
The water-stream do gently flow;
An’ willow-boughs do hang vull low
To touch the cool an’ glassen tide,
Where bright the yellow clote do grow,
A-floaten on the river-side.

Wi’ cup o’ gould an’ leafe o’ green,
Her head do rest upon the deep,
The fairest blossom ever seen
Where shade o’ alder-trees do creep.
Her goulden petels open wide,
To catch the zun-beams as they vall,
An’ float upon the quiet tide,
The sweetest water-flower o’ all.

The dragon-fly wi' wings o’ blue
Do dart around her shining crown,
While reed-birds zing their zongs anew
As shade o’ eve do zettle down.
The cattle, coming down to drink,
Do splash their veet in shingle grey,
An’ zeek the water's coolin' brink
To pass the heat o’ zummer day.

Oh, zweet bright clote! when winter chill
Do freeze the stream an' strip the bough,
An’ dark an’ drear do stand the hill,
My heart shall zee thee bright as now:
A-shinin' on the river-brim,
In Dorset meäds where waters glide,
A goulden light when days be dim,
A-dancin' on the zummer tide.

***

*Note: In 19th-century Dorset dialect (as preserved by rural poets like William Barnes), "clote" is the traditional name for the yellow water-lily.*

counterfactuals.prompt: write a rustic poem about a river flower in dorset dialect
counterfactuals.output:
**The Yellow Vlower o’ the Frome**

Where clear the quiet Frome do rinn,
Beneath the shade o’ willow tree,
A-gleamin’ in the zummer zun,
As vresh an’ vair as bloom can be;
Down by the reedy brim zo low,
A golden vlower do gently blow.

Her tall green blades, like zwords o’ sedge,
Do guard her head o’ bright yallow,
Right on the river’s rushy edge,
Where coolin' waters ripple slow.
An’ wind do whisper drough the grass,
To kiss the vlower as er do pass.

The bumble-bee do come an’ hum,
A-buzzin’ round her crown o' gold,
Vor zweetest honey he do come,
A-vore the warm day do grow cold;
An' trout do dart beneath her shade,
In dark, still nooks the stream hath made.

Let town-volk bide in smoke an’ din,
An’ fret their lives with cark an’ care,
Gi’e me the mead where peace be in,
An’ water-clotes do bloom zo fair.
Beside the stream in Dorset land,
A-growin’ vresh vrom Nature’s hand.

***

*Glossary of Dorset Terms:*
* **Frome** – A major river in Dorset  
* **Rinn** – Run  
* **Zummer / Zun** – Summer / Sun  
* **Vresh / Vair / Vlower** – Fresh / Fair / Flower  
* **Brim** – Bank/edge of a river  
* **Zwords** – Swords  
* **Drough** – Through  
* **Er** – It / She  
* **A-vore** – Before  
* **Mead** – Meadow  
* **Water-clote** – Dorset dialect name for the water-lily or yellow water-iris  
* **Cark** – Worry/trouble
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

*Where the yellow clotes do vloat upon the brook.*

An’ dive deep down beneath the glassy pool,  
To wash the dust an’ heat vrom off the skin,  
Wi’ merry laugh an’ splashin’ out an’ in,  
*Where the yellow clotes do vloat upon the brook.*

An’ watch the water softly creep an’ glide,  
To mark the golden blossoms, broad an’ bright,  
A-basken in the noon-day’s blazin’ light,  
*Where the yellow clotes do vloat upon the brook.*  

Now dusk do vall, the hay is stacked an’ dry,  
An’ stars do peep across the zummer sky;

To close a long hard day o’ zummer heat,  
*Where the yellow clotes do vloat upon the brook.*

**The Beästs Among the Clotes**

When zultry heat o’ Zummer day
Do bake the grass in sunny mead,
An’ drouth do turn the clover gray,

An’ warm hides steaming in the sun,
Do leave the vields so parched an’ dry,
Down where the shaded waters run.

To reach the river’s coolin’ brim,
Where alder-boughs above their head
Do make the bright day zoft an’ dim.

To feel the clear fresh water flow,
An’ take a long an' quiet sip.

An' floating on the water’s breäst,
The yellow clotes* do lay an’ gleam,
Wi' broad green leaves in tranquil rest,
A-swayen gently wi' the stream.
The red cows push their wet snouts near
The lily-blossoms open wide,
While ripples circle zoft an’ clear,
To touch the grassy river-side.

How sweet to mark, in noon-tide hours,
The kine a-stonden in the lew,
Among the golden water-flow’rs,
Wi' skies above o’ brightish blue;
To hear the water murmur by,
Where clotes do float an' reeds do shake,
An’ feel the gentle countryside
A-sleepen by the quiet lake.

***
